newsitem.title: CROATIA: Tudjman says vote starts Serb-Croat co-existence.
newsitem.headline: Tudjman says vote starts Serb-Croat co-existence.

text.p: President Franjo Tudjman said in a strikingly conciliatory message on Thursday that regional elections this weekend would launch a new era for minority Serbs as equal citizens in Croatia.

The authoritarian nationalist leader said the inclusion of the Serb enclave of Eastern Slavonia in Sunday's countrywide county and municipal elections to speed its "reintegration" with the rest of Croatia was an historic accomplishment.

"This is a year of the return and reconciliation of all Croatian citizens," Tudjman said, referring both to Serbs in Eastern Slavonia and Croats expelled from it during a 1991 war but now keen to reclaim their former homes.

"The elections also present the start of a peaceful life for Serbs as equal citizens of Croatia," Tudjman told reporters after pre-election talks with the U.N. transitional administrator for Eastern Slavonia, Jacques Klein, who stood beside him.
"Serbs who are willing to recognise and accept Croatia's constitution and laws can stay and contribute to our economic, social and cultural development," Tudjman said.
"Their civic rights, home and property are guaranteed by our constitution in line with the highest standards. This is the end of the (six-year-long) state of war.

"Our victory was secured at the highest price with huge loss of life and terrible damage done to our economy. I call upon all our citizens to heal the wounds of the past and put all their efforts into building the future."
Croatian state institutions offering proportional representation to Serbs will be phased in over a three-month period after the elections.
The United Nations' administrative mandate for Eastern Slavonia ends on July 15 and 5,000 U.N. peacekeeping troops will then withdraw.
Minority Serbs seized the fertile, oil-rich region and two other enclaves in a 1991 insurrection against Croatia's move to independence from Serbian-led federal Yugoslavia.

Croatia recaptured two western enclaves in blitz offensives by government troops over U.N. truce lines but agreed under Western diplomatic pressure to gradual reintegration of Eastern Slavonia under U.N. supervision.

Zagreb has pledged significant minority rights to Eastern Slavonia's Serbs and slashed an inflated list of Serb war crime suspects down to 150 names to help satisfy Western conditions for urgent reconstruction aid in the war-battered region.
The U.N. Transitional Authority (UNTAES) is striving to revive Eastern Slavonia's pre-1991 multi-ethnic society.

But many Serbs, while signing up for Croatian citizenship papers qualifying them to vote, remain sceptical of Croatian intentions. Western monitors report persistent local persecution of Serbs who remained in areas reconquered in 1995.
Many Croats who were displaced insist they can not foresee living again with Serb neighbours. The leader of the Croat refugee association is an anti-Serb rightist.

Anywhere from a quarter to a half of the Serb population, if not more, is likely to leave for nearby Serbia after the vote because they are unreconciled to the return of Croatian rule or fearful of retribution for violence against Croats.

Almost half the estimated 120,000 Serbs in Eastern Slavonia are refugees. They will have to cede housing to returning Croat owners but face grave obstacles going back to homes in western Croatia destroyed or now occupied by Croats.
